situation:
You are the operations manager for HOLLAND & DAUGHTERS HARDWARE, a six-store hardware chain now run by the founding family's third generation. The president (judge) has asked you to recommend how the stores should be staffed, with this year's rent, insurance and utility costs coming in higher than any year before.

Sales have held flat while those costs climbed at every location. One shift carries the chain: Saturday morning produces close to a third of a store's weekly sales, and the crew that works it is the most experienced group the company has. Weekday evenings, from six to nine, are the quietest hours in every store.

Closing at six and moving those hours to the weekend is fully within the company's rights and would cut the payroll and the lighting the evenings consume. Contractors have shopped after their job sites close for three generations, and the part-time staff who work evenings would lose those hours. Keeping the doors open protects both and leaves the higher costs to be recovered somewhere else.

The president (judge) wants your analysis of whether the stores should close at six, and of how the decision should be explained to the people it costs the most. The president (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas, and will thank you after your presentation and questions.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the president (judge) of HOLLAND & DAUGHTERS HARDWARE. Business background is the same as the situation above.

You have asked the operations manager to recommend whether the chain should close its stores at six o'clock and move those hours to Saturday, and to explain how that decision would be carried to the contractors and the part-time evening staff it costs the most.

You will greet the participant, ask to hear their ideas, and after the presentation you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: What should we say to the evening staff whose hours we are cutting?
How should a contractor who complains at the service desk hear about this?
